clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant haemolytic anaemia in which red cells are overhydrated and swollen, associated with mutations in RHAG (Rh-associated glycoprotein)
The blood film shows numerous stomatocytes with a central slit-like pallor
Red cells are overhydrated with a low mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration and a raised mean cell volume, the mirror image of dehydrated xerocytosis
Osmotic fragility is characteristically increased because the swollen cells lyse readily
Loss of stomatin from the red-cell membrane is a recognised biochemical feature
Anaemia is usually moderate with reticulocytosis and variable jaundice and splenomegaly
As in other hereditary stomatocytoses, splenectomy carries a high risk of thromboembolic complications and is generally avoided
Diagnosis combines red-cell indices, ektacytometry, membrane protein analysis, and genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: In overhydrated hereditary stomatocytosis, mutations in RHAG convert the Rh-associated glycoprotein into an abnormally permeable cation-conducting pore, greatly increasing monovalent cation flux across the red-cell membrane. Net cation and water gain overhydrate and swell the cell, lowering its haemoglobin concentration and producing the characteristic stomatocyte morphology with associated loss of the membrane protein stomatin. The fragile, overhydrated cells undergo premature destruction, causing a chronic haemolytic anaemia; as with related disorders, splenectomy is hazardous because it predisposes to thrombosis.
additionalDifferentials: Rh-null disease and related membrane defects
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and reticulocytes noting a low mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration and high mean cell volume
Peripheral blood film showing prominent stomatocytes
Osmotic gradient ektacytometry demonstrating the overhydrated red-cell profile
Red-cell membrane protein analysis for reduced stomatin
redFlags: Severe or decompensated anaemia during intercurrent illness or aplastic crisis
Progressive iron overload with organ involvement
Rapidly enlarging spleen or evidence of hypersplenism
reference.prognosis: The chronic haemolytic anaemia is usually moderate and compatible with a good quality of life, but the major avoidable hazard is post-splenectomy thrombosis, and iron overload requires monitoring.
pitfalls: Recommending splenectomy without recognising the marked post-splenectomy thrombotic risk of hereditary stomatocytoses
Confusing overhydrated with dehydrated stomatocytosis despite opposite red-cell indices and fragility
Missing the diagnosis when stomatocytes are attributed to an artefact or to acquired causes
Failing to monitor and manage iron overload in a non-transfused patient
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Avoid splenectomy, which is contraindicated because it markedly increases thrombotic risk in this and related stomatocytosis disorders
Give folic acid supplementation to support the increased erythropoiesis of chronic haemolysis
Provide red-cell transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, restricting it to clinical need
Monitor for and manage iron overload, using iron chelation where transfusional or absorptive loading develops, and avoid unnecessary iron supplementation
Track the full blood count, reticulocytes, haemolysis markers and iron studies over time
Consider thromboprophylaxis around surgery or periods of immobility given the underlying prothrombotic tendency
Offer genetic counselling and family assessment for this autosomal dominant RHAG-related disorder
